Ru7B3 forms in a non-centrosymmetric hexagonal Th7Fe3-type crystal structure with the space group P63mc.
The superconducting transition temperature (Tc) of the Ru7B3 single crystals was around 2.6 K, lower than the 3.2 K observed for the polycrystalline starting material.
The lower critical field Hc1(0) was estimated to be around 30 Oe for the [100] direction and 43 Oe for the [001] direction of the Ru7B3 single crystals.

The researchers were unable to fit the temperature dependence of the upper critical field Hc2(T) to the Werthamer-Helfand-Hohenberg (WHH) model, estimating Hc2(0) to be around 16 kOe for the [100] direction and 9.5 kOe for the [001] direction.
The researchers grew Ru7B3 single crystals using both natural boron (B) and the isotopically enriched 11B, the latter being suitable for neutron scattering experiments.
The floating zone technique with an optical mirror furnace equipped with high-power xenon arc lamps was used to grow the Ru7B3 single crystals, requiring slow growth rates of around 3 mm/h.
Laue X-ray diffraction was used to examine the quality of the as-grown Ru7B3 crystals and to cut slices along specific crystallographic directions for further measurements.

The lower superconducting transition temperature Tc of the Ru7B3 single crystals compared to the polycrystalline samples is often associated with loss of boron during the crystal growth process and the presence of boron vacancies.

The motivation for studying the non-centrosymmetric superconductor Ru7B3 is its complex superconducting properties, which can differ from conventional superconductors due to the lack of inversion symmetry in the crystal structure.
The researchers found that slow growth rates were necessary to obtain the best quality Ru7B3 single crystals using the floating zone technique.

The Ru7B3 single crystals grown with the 11B isotope have a much lower neutron absorption cross-section, making them suitable for neutron scattering experiments to investigate the vortex state of this non-centrosymmetric superconductor.
The researchers observed a greater degree of anisotropy in the upper critical field Hc2(0) values for the Ru7B3 single crystals compared to previous reports.
The Ru7B3 compound melts congruently at around 1600°C, making it suitable for crystal growth by the floating zone technique.
The as-grown Ru7B3 crystal boules had shiny surfaces with a golden lustre and were large enough (40-50 mm long, 4-6 mm diameter) for detailed physical property measurements.
The researchers used spark erosion to cut slices from the Ru7B3 crystal boules for magnetization and resistivity measurements.
